summary:
Valle del Cauca sits under Colombia's national framework, which is among the more developed legal regimes for trans people in Latin America. Since a rule change approved in June 2015, trans Colombians change the sex marker on government-issued identification by signing a document before a notary, replacing the earlier route under which judges ordered bodily inspections or psychiatric assessments. Constitutional Court jurisprudence dating from 1993 recognises legal gender recognition on the basis of self-recognition without a surgical requirement. Marriage equality has been available since 2016, adoption by same-sex couples since 2015, and national identification documents have carried "trans" and "non-binary" markers from November 2025. A comprehensive trans law was still under legislative consideration in 2025. These instruments are national; the sources located for this department contain no departmental ordinance, statute or enforcement series of its own.

The department's safety picture is worse than the national average. Caribe Afirmativo's 2025 assessment places Valle del Cauca among the departments where what it describes as a territorial expansion of violence applies: killings have spread outward from established hotspots while the state response has remained insufficient. Lethal anti-trans violence in Colombia now occurs openly in urban settings as well as in territories held by armed actors. Sara Millerey, a 32-year-old trans woman, was attacked in broad daylight in Bello, Antioquia, on 4 April 2025; a video of the assault went viral from the following day and she died that afternoon. Police interrogated local residents, and even after President Petro ordered an urgent investigation no arrest had been made.

Official recorded figures are high. The Attorney General's Office recorded 35 LGBTI murders in Colombia between January and May 2025 alone, and the state ombudsman counted at least 25 trans women murdered between January and September 2025. Caribe Afirmativo recorded one LGBTIQ+ person killed every 32 hours across 2025, a 63% increase over 2024 (270 killings against 164), with trans women accounting for 18% of the 2024 homicides. One report counted 13 trans people killed in the first quarter of 2025, and EL PAÍS cited additional killings of gay men and the stabbing death of a trans rough-sleeper in the same period. Earlier counts reported 41 trans people killed in Colombia in 2023 and eight trans women killed between February and April 2024.

The UN Independent Expert on sexual orientation and gender identity, Graeme Reid, completed a fact-finding mission across several Colombian cities in May 2025. He praised the government's legal reforms and stated commitment to equality while warning that institutional progress and daily lived experience are disconnected, and that widespread discrimination and violence against LGBT people must be addressed urgently as killings rise. Some of this violence has been prosecuted as an international crime rather than ordinary homicide: in July 2023 the Special Jurisdiction for Peace indicted 15 former rebels for war crimes and crimes against humanity against people of diverse sexual orientations and gender identities, with the state acknowledging that conflict-driven violence against these individuals constitutes gender persecution, a crime against humanity. The UN Human Rights Committee has registered concern over the same pattern.
tangentialFactors:
Where armed groups operate, the risk to trans women rises sharply. In the department of Caquetá, armed groups ran "social cleansing" campaigns announced through street and WhatsApp flyer campaigns naming "drug addicts, prostitutes and faggots" as legitimate military targets, and threatened a further wave. In the department of Guajira, armed groups posted flyers from March 2024 carrying a kill list of named individuals under the wording "All will be military targets... homosexuals, lesbians, rapists, trans". Valle del Cauca does not appear in either account, but the pattern those departments demonstrate — lethal threat from armed actors, published lists, and forced displacement — is the wider pattern Caribe Afirmativo's 2025 assessment applies to this department.

Economic marginalisation compounds the violence risk. In Caquetá, trans women reported that discrimination limited them mainly to hairdressing or sex work, and one trans salon owner was forced to relocate twice after receiving death threats from armed men; a friend of another trans woman in that department was killed. Displacement has been the outcome for trans women who resisted threats elsewhere too, including a trans woman and local election candidate who was told by three armed men she had one week to leave town, hid for a week, then fled at night.

The Colombian courts have intervened directly in detention, ruling on the treatment of a trans woman deprived of liberty and protecting the rights of trans detainees in the prison system. Detention conditions remain a live risk area for trans visitors and residents alike, in this department as nationally.
localsOnly:
Colombia's trans-specific legal and health machinery is available to residents of Valle del Cauca on the same national terms as elsewhere: the notarial route to changing the sex marker on identification documents has been in place since 2015, and self-recognition-based legal recognition has been constitutional jurisprudence since 1993. National identification documents have carried "trans" and "non-binary" markers since November 2025, which affects how residents present in every administrative and health encounter.

For residents, the operational reality is that departmental authorities have produced no specific protective ordinance or enforcement series identified in the sources reviewed. Protection has arrived instead through national institutional channels: the ombudsman's homicide counts, the Attorney General's murder figures, and judicial intervention in trans detainees' rights. Residents reporting threats, displacement or targeted violence would therefore be working through national bodies rather than a departmental mechanism.

Caribe Afirmativo's 2025 monitoring places Valle del Cauca within the outward spread of lethal violence against LGBTIQ+ people, with a state response described as insufficient. That assessment is relevant to residents because it characterises the local enforcement environment, not only the national one.
outOfScopeNotes:
No departmental statute, ordinance, decree or enforcement series specific to Valle del Cauca was found in the sources reviewed. The department's entry rests on its place within Caribe Afirmativo's 2025 departmental counts and on the national framework, which applies in full here. Whether any Valle del Cauca-specific measure exists outside these sources is unresolved.

The violence incidents documented in the source inventory occurred in other departments — Caquetá, Guajira, Antioquia — and are carried in this record as national context and as the pattern the departmental assessment rests on. Whether any named armed-group campaign, flyer initiative or kill list has operated within Valle del Cauca itself is unresolved; no source reviewed states this either way.

The exact current status of the comprehensive trans law under legislative consideration in 2025 is unresolved, as is whether the November 2025 marker changes on identification documents have been implemented in departmental offices without obstruction. The gap between the Attorney General's figures, the ombudsman's counts and civil-society tallies also remains unresolved as a measurement question, though each independently records a high level of lethal anti-trans violence.
